This year's theme, restoring trust,
managing transformation, a united
nations that delivers for all, captures
the task before us.
Trust will not be restored by words
alone. It will be restored by what this
organization delivers for every country,
large or small.
37 years ago, the mods asked this
assembly to face a simple truth.
That small state can be highly
vulnerable to external threats and acts
of influence.
In response, this assembly adopted
resolution 4451,
an initiative led by the Maldives,
affirming the importance of protecting
the sovereignty and territorial
integrity of small states.
That was true then and it is true even
today. But the threats have evolved.
Insecurity now travels through sea
lanes, supply chains, financial markets,
digital networks and new technologies.
Today, sovereignty can be weakened
without a single border being crossed.
It can be undermined when external
powers limit a state's freedom to
choose.
This is why the Morris comes before this
assembly with a clear message. Every
state large or small must have the
freedom and capacity to shape its own
future.
A sovereign future and that future
begins with peace.
The Indian Ocean must remain peaceful.
It must remain as a region where trade
can flow and where states can prosper.
Regional competition among major powers
must not limit the choices of smaller
states.
Conflict does not have to reach our
shores to affect us.
In today's interconnected world, a
crisis far away can quickly become a
crisis at home.
Interruption to maritime traffic through
the state of Hormones raises fuel
prices. It affects food supplies and air
travel.
The consequences of these are felt
across tourism and public finances in
the Maldives.
The mod therefore condemns the closure
of the state of Hormuz.
The state must remain open and safe.
The modest father condemns the attack
attacks on Saudi Arabia, United Arab
Emirates, Bahrain, Gatar, Kuwait, Oman
and Jordan.
The modus appreciates the diplomatic
efforts of Oman, Pakistan and gut to

The right to offer, the right to a
sovereign future must belong to all. And
nowhere is that right more brutally
denied than in Palestine.
Is genocide and war crimes against
Palestinian continue and their actions
are not confined to Gaza.
Its military attacks across the region
have violated the sovereignty of other
states.
Security cannot be built by exporting
insecurity.
Nor can any country demand respect for
its sovereignty while violating the
sovereignty of others.
No state should be shielded from
accountability by its power or political
alliances.
But condemnation alone is not enough.
Every member state must ask what have we
done to end this violence.
The United Nations must ask itself the
same question.
The problem is not a lack of law. The
rules are clear. What is absent is equal
application.
humanitarians.
International law cannot bind the weak
and bend for the powerful. The same
rules, the same standard, no exception.
Israel's genocide in Gaza must end.
Israel's illegal occupation of Palestine
and other Arab lands must end. Illegal
settlements must end. Humanitarian
assistance must reach Palestinians
safely, rapidly and at scale.
International courts and other and the
resolution of this organization must be
respected and implemented
for the Palestinian people. A sovereign
future means freedom, dignity,
self-determination, and the right to
live their security in their own state.
The Morris will always stand with
Palestinian people and their undeniable
right for that future.
This is why I reiterate our call for the
recognition of independent and sovereign
state of Palestine based on the pre967
borders with East Jerusalem as its
capital.
And if this organization is restored
trust and deliver for all, Palestine
must become a full member of the United
Nations.
Conflict is not the only threat to
sovereignty. Forces beyond our borders
can also limit a state's freedom to
shape its own future.
For seeds like the Maldives, none is
more consequential than climate change.
For seeds, climate change is altering
the very fiscal foundations of our
nations.
Sea level rise is therefore not simply
an environmental concern. It is a matter
of national planning and national
security. It is a matter of sovereignty.
Let there be no doubt. Rising seas may
alter our shores, but they will not
erase our statethood. They will not
reduce our rights. They will not weaken
our maritime entitlements.
and they will not diminish our national
agency.
Our response must be to adapt, innovate
and build.
But resilience demands the means to act.
That means finance must reach those who
need it at the scale, at the speed, and
on the terms needed to build resilience.
This is why COP 31 in Antholia must be a
cope of delivery.
Implementation must be the measure of
commitment.
We must we must move faster. We must

For island nations that progress cannot

only when they enable progress at home.
His Excellency President Dr. Muhammad
Moizu has set a clear ambition.
Furthermore is to become a developed
country by 2040.
We are pursuing that goal by rising
productivity, diversifying our economy,
building resilient infrastructure,
expanding renewable energy and investing
in our people. Our future will be built
by moldivians.
But the international system can widen
or narrow our choices.
Technology transfer, resilient supply
chains and accessible finance expand
choice.
Techn technological dependence, external
shocks and unsustainable debt limits it.
This is why reform of the international
financial architecture matters.
We must implement the sea commitment and
deliver on its promises on finance, debt
and reform.
Earlier this year, the mods joined other
developing countries in launching the
Brows platform.
It must become a lasting mechanism that

place in the financial system but a
voice in shaping it.
But for seeds, greater agency also

We must build our institutions, improve
stability and attract responsible
investment and meaningful partnerships.
And these partnerships must build
national capacity and support national
ambitions.
Partnerships must solve national needs,
strengthen what we have and leave us
more capable than before. Our shared
challenges can become a shared
opportunities.
This is the spirit of President Dr.
Muhammad Moiz's mold's first policy.
Partnership built around respect,
national interest and mutual
contribution
and the same principle must guide the
technological transformation before us.
Artificial intelligence offers
significant opportunities for small
states. AI can close distance. It can
help overcome scale
and it can put better health care,
education and public services within
reach.
But these opportunities must be shared.
Every country must have a voice in
shaping the global roles for AI.
The digital future should strengthen our
ability to serve our people better, not
create new forms of dependence.
And as the world transform, so must the
United Nations.
The UN80 initiative is an opportunity to
reduce duplication, improve
accountability, and focus resources on
results.
But efficiency must not be measured
simply by what we cut. It must be
measured by what we deliver.
And the United Nation must not retreat
from the countries that need it most in
the name of efficiency.
Reform must preserve a meaningful UN
presence on the ground particularly in
seats.
The UN development system must respond
to the needs of program countries and
remain guided by relevant international
frameworks.
The reform process must be member
stateled. It must include must be
inclusive and and transparent.
This is how reform will restore trust by
bring the United Nations closer to the
people in the countries it serves.
Reform must also confront one of this
organization oldest weaknesses, unequal
representation.
The security council cannot reflect the
world of 1945 while deciding for the
world of today.
It must be expanded in both permanent
and non-permanmanent categories.
Seats must have a rotarian seat.
Africa must receive the represent
representation long denied to it and the
veto must be abolished.
After all, representation is not merely
symbolic.
Who sits at the table shapes what the
table sees.
Small states understand how closely
climate, finance, trade, supply chains
and security are connected. We also know
that international law is our strongest
safeguard against unequal power.
That principle must remain at the heart
of the international system.
The molds will take its seat on the

We do so because small states must be
decision makers, not decision takers.
Representation matters not only within
the bodies of this organization but also
in its leadership.
As Secretary General Gutes approaches
the end of a decade of service, the Mais
thank him for his leadership and
commitment to international cooperation.
The process to choose his successor must
be transparent and based on merit. It
must draw from the full breath of talent
available to this organization.
For more than eight decades, every
secretary general has been a man.
It is time for woman to lead this
organization.
A leader who will defend the charter
without exception.
Who can turn reform into delivery
and who will listen to all member states
including smallest.
The task ahead is immense. The choice we

assembly do?
The modus proposes a simple test for a
sovereign future.
When we act on conflict, climate,
finance, technology or institutional
reform, let us ask
does this decision expand a status
freedom tools? Does it build national
capacity and reduce dependence?
Does it protect sovereignty and
independence decision making? If the
answer is no, we must change course
and we must hold every state to the same
standard.
Let this be the measure of n
international cooperation. Not what we
promise but what we make possible.
This is the measure of a united nations
that delivers for all.
In 1989, the modest asked this assembly
to protect small states from external
threats.
Today, we ask it to protect something
just as fundamental. Every state's
freedom to choose choose its own future.
A future chosen by its people. A future
grounded in international law. a
sovereign future for every state. I
